title: Unit 7: Reproduction in Animals and Plants

questions.question: Where does Spermatogenesis take place inside the human testes?
questions.explanation: Spermatogenesis occurs in the walls of the seminiferous tubules, progressing from basement membrane spermatogonia to lumen spermatozoa.

questions.question: Which large somatic cells in the seminiferous tubules provide structural support, nutrition, and blood-testis barrier protection to developing germ cells?
questions.explanation: Sertoli cells nurse developing sperm, phagocytose excess cytoplasm, secrete inhibin, and form the tight-junction blood-testis barrier.

questions.question: Which cells located in the interstitial connective tissue between seminiferous tubules synthesize and secrete Testosterone under the stimulation of LH?
questions.explanation: Leydig cells respond to Luteinizing Hormone (LH/ICSH) by synthesizing and secreting androgens (primarily testosterone).

questions.question: How many functional, flagellated haploid spermatozoa are produced from one single diploid Primary Spermatocyte following meiotic division?
questions.explanation: A primary spermatocyte ($2n$) undergoes meiosis I to form two secondary spermatocytes ($n$), which undergo meiosis II to form 4 functional spermatids ($n$).

questions.question: What is the cap-like lysosome-derived structure on the anterior head of a mature sperm cell that contains hydrolytic enzymes (hyaluronidase, acrosin) to penetrate the ovum?
questions.explanation: The acrosome contains hydrolytic enzymes released during the acrosome reaction to digest the zona pellucida and corona radiata of the egg.

questions.question: Where are mature spermatozoa stored, and where do they acquire forward motility and fertilizing capacity over a period of 10 to 14 days?
questions.explanation: Sperm exit the testis non-motile and acquire maturation, motility, and surface membrane modifications while moving through the epididymis.

questions.question: Which accessory male reproductive glands produce approximately 60% of the seminal fluid volume, rich in fructose, prostaglandins, and coagulating enzymes?
questions.explanation: Seminal vesicles secrete alkaline fructose-rich fluid that provides an energy substrate for sperm motility and prostaglandins for uterine contractions.

questions.question: What is the primary role of the slightly acidic fluid secreted by the Prostate Gland containing citrate and prostate-specific antigen (PSA)?

options.A: Liquefying the seminal coagulum after ejaculation and nourishing sperm
options.C: Lubricating the glans penis before intercourse

questions.explanation: Prostatic fluid contains proteolytic enzymes (like PSA) that liquefy clotted semen within 15–30 minutes, freeing sperm to swim into the cervix.

questions.question: Where does human Oogenesis halt (meiotic arrest) during embryonic development before birth?

options.A: Prophase I of Meiosis I (in Dictyate / Diplotene stage)

questions.explanation: Primary oocytes enter meiosis I during fetal life and remain arrested at prophase I (diplotene) until puberty, when hormonal surges resume maturation.

questions.question: At what stage of division is the Secondary Oocyte arrested when it is ovulated from the Graafian follicle into the Fallopian tube?
questions.explanation: The ovulated secondary oocyte is arrested at Metaphase II, completing meiosis II only if penetrated by a fertilizing sperm.

questions.question: How many functional ova are produced from one diploid Primary Oocyte during human female oogenesis?

options.A: 1 functional ovum (and up to 3 non-functional polar bodies)

questions.explanation: Asymmetric cytokinesis retains virtually all nutrient cytoplasm in one large functional ovum, discarding excess haploid genomes as polar bodies.

questions.question: In an average 28-day human menstrual cycle, on which day does Ovulation typically occur, triggered by a sharp surge in Luteinizing Hormone (LH)?
questions.explanation: Rising estrogen from the Graafian follicle triggers an LH surge at mid-cycle (around day 14), inducing follicular rupture and ovulation.

questions.question: What temporary endocrine gland develops from the collapsed, ruptured Graafian follicle after ovulation under the influence of LH?
questions.explanation: The ruptured follicle transforms into the glandular Corpus Luteum, secreting large amounts of progesterone to maintain pregnancy.

questions.question: If fertilization does NOT occur, what happens to the Corpus Luteum approximately 10 to 12 days after ovulation?

options.A: It degenerates into a white fibrous scar called the Corpus Albicans, causing progesterone levels to plunge and triggering Menstruation
options.C: It continues to grow and releases hCG

questions.explanation: Without hCG from an implanted embryo, the corpus luteum atrophies into a corpus albicans; falling progesterone causes the endometrium to slough (menses).

questions.question: What is the typical site of Fertilization (union of sperm and secondary oocyte) in the human female reproductive tract?
questions.explanation: Fertilization normally takes place in the ampulla, the widest and longest section of the Fallopian tube.

questions.question: What is the 'Cortical Reaction' (Slow Block to Polyspermy) that occurs immediately following sperm-egg membrane fusion?

options.A: Exocytosis of cortical granules releasing enzymes that harden the Zona Pellucida and destroy sperm receptors, preventing multiple sperm entry
options.B: Instant depolarization of the egg membrane via sodium ions
options.D: Expulsion of the zygote into the vagina

questions.explanation: Intracellular $Ca^{2+}$ release causes cortical granules to exocytose enzymes, hardening the zona pellucida (zona reaction) to permanently block polyspermy.

questions.question: Which hormone is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast of the implanted blastocyst, maintaining the corpus luteum and detected in pregnancy tests?
questions.explanation: hCG rescues the corpus luteum to preserve progesterone production, forming the biochemical basis for home urine pregnancy dipstick tests.

questions.question: What is the thick, glycoprotein coat surrounding the plasma membrane of a mammalian secondary oocyte?
questions.explanation: The zona pellucida is an extracellular matrix of glycoproteins (ZP1, ZP2, ZP3) that binds sperm and mediates the acrosome reaction.

questions.question: What is 'Capacitation' of mammalian spermatozoa?

options.A: The physiological biochemical conditioning of sperm occurring inside the female tract (cholesterol removal, hyperactivation) necessary for fertilization
options.B: The production of flagella in the testis
options.C: The storage of sperm in liquid nitrogen

questions.explanation: Capacitation takes several hours in the female reproductive tract, stripping surface sterols and glycoproteins to allow the acrosome reaction.

questions.question: What is the permanent cessation of the primary ovarian functions and menstrual cycles in women (typically occurring between 45–55 years) called?
questions.explanation: Menopause marks the end of female reproductive life due to depletion of functional ovarian follicles and a decline in estrogen/progesterone.

questions.question: What is 'Menarche'?

options.A: The very first occurrence of menstruation in an adolescent female at puberty
options.B: The onset of menopause in older women
options.C: A missed menstrual period during pregnancy

questions.explanation: Menarche is the initial menstrual bleeding marking female puberty, typically occurring around ages 11–14.

questions.question: In angiosperm plants, what are the male and female reproductive organs called?

options.A: Stamen (male: anther + filament) and Carpel/Pistil (female: stigma, style, ovary)

questions.explanation: The stamen is the androecium (microsporophyll) and the carpel/pistil is the gynoecium (megasporophyll) of flowering plants.

questions.question: What is 'Double Fertilization' in flowering plants (angiosperms)?

options.A: One male sperm nucleus fertilizes the haploid egg to form the diploid zygote ($2n$), while the second sperm fuses with two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm ($3n$)
options.B: Two separate pollen tubes entering two different flowers
options.C: Fertilization of two seeds in one fruit
options.D: A flower that pollinates itself twice in a season

questions.explanation: Double fertilization is unique to angiosperms: Syngamy produces the $2n$ zygote, and triple fusion produces the $3n$ nutritive endosperm tissue.

questions.question: What is the ploidy level of the Endosperm tissue in typical Angiosperm seeds?
questions.explanation: Triple fusion involves one haploid sperm ($1n$) fusing with the central cell containing two haploid polar nuclei ($1n + 1n$), creating a $3n$ endosperm.

questions.question: What is 'Pollination'?

options.A: The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the receptive stigma of a flower
options.B: The fusion of sperm and egg nuclei in the embryo sac
options.C: The germination of seeds in damp soil
options.D: The shedding of flower petals in autumn

questions.explanation: Pollination is the mechanical transfer of pollen (by wind, insects, water, or birds) from anther to stigma prior to fertilization.

questions.question: What is 'Parthenogenesis' in animal reproduction?

options.A: A form of asexual reproduction in which an unfertilized egg develops into a complete, viable offspring (e.g., in honeybee drones, aphids, some lizards)
options.B: The fusion of two sperm with one egg

questions.explanation: Parthenogenesis ('virgin birth') produces offspring without fertilization (e.g., haploid male honeybees developing from unfertilized queen eggs).

questions.question: What is 'Parthenocarpy' in botanical horticulture?

options.A: The development of a fruit without prior fertilization of ovules, resulting in naturally seedless fruit (e.g., commercial bananas, seedless grapes)
options.B: The germination of seeds while still attached to the parent plant (vivipary)

questions.explanation: Parthenocarpy produces seedless fruits naturally or via auxin/gibberellin application without ovule fertilization.

questions.question: Which sexually transmitted infection (STI) is caused by the spirochete bacterium Treponema pallidum, characterized by a painless chancre in primary stages?
questions.explanation: Syphilis progresses from primary chancre to secondary rash/condylomata, and potentially to tertiary neurosyphilis/gummas if untreated.

questions.question: Which sexually transmitted disease is caused by the Gram-negative diplococcus Neisseria gonorrhoeae, causing purulent urethral discharge and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)?
questions.explanation: Gonorrhea infects mucosal linings, causing painful purulent urethritis in males and cervicitis/PID in females.

questions.question: What is the causative agent of Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS), which infects and destroys CD4+ T-helper lymphocytes?
questions.explanation: HIV is an enveloped retrovirus that binds CD4 and CCR5/CXCR4 receptors on helper T-cells, progressively destroying cell-mediated immunity.

questions.question: Which surgical procedure involves severing and tying the male vas deferens to achieve permanent male sterilization?
questions.explanation: Vasectomy ligates the vas deferens, preventing sperm from entering the ejaculate while preserving normal testosterone and semen volume.

questions.question: What is 'In Vitro Fertilization' (IVF)?

options.A: An assisted reproductive technology where ova are extracted and fertilized by sperm in a laboratory dish before transferring the embryo into the uterus
options.B: Cloning an animal from somatic adult skin cells
options.C: Artificially inseminating cattle in dairy barns
options.D: Treating infertility exclusively with herbal vitamins

questions.explanation: IVF involves ovarian hyperstimulation, oocyte retrieval, external petridish fertilization, culture to blastocyst, and intrauterine embryo transfer.

questions.question: In plant tissue culture, what is 'Micropropagation'?

options.A: The in vitro propagation of large numbers of genetically identical plants (clones) from small explants cultured on nutrient media under sterile conditions
options.B: Growing giant trees in natural forests
options.C: Spraying synthetic pesticides on agricultural crops

questions.explanation: Micropropagation uses totipotent plant cells in sterile media supplemented with auxins/cytokinins to produce millions of disease-free clonal plantlets.

questions.question: What is 'Apomixis' in botany?

options.A: The asexual formation of seeds without meiosis or syngamy, yielding seedlings that are maternal genetic clones (e.g., in dandelions and citrus)
options.B: The rotting of seeds in overwatered soil
options.C: Pollination performed by bats at night
options.D: The cross-breeding of two distant plant genera

questions.explanation: Apomixis bypasses meiosis and fertilization, allowing maternal cells of the ovule to develop directly into an embryo within the seed.

questions.question: What is the structural role of the Scrotum in human male reproductive physiology?

options.A: Holding the testes outside the abdominal cavity at a temperature 2°C to 3°C lower than core body temperature for optimal spermatogenesis

questions.explanation: Spermatogenesis requires temperatures below 37°C (~34–35°C), regulated by the dartos and cremaster muscles of the scrotal sac.
